title: Chapter I
paragraphs: 1801—I have just come back from visiting my landlord—the only neighbour I shall have to put up with. This is certainly beautiful country! Nowhere in England, I believe, could I have chosen a place so entirely cut off from the bustle of society. A perfect heaven for a man who hates company—and Mr. Heathcliff and I make an excellent pair to share its desolation. A splendid fellow! He had no idea how warmly I felt towards him when, as I rode up, I saw his black eyes retreat so suspiciously beneath their brows, and when, on hearing my name, his fingers burrowed still deeper into his waistcoat, determined to guard their privacy.
“Mr. Heathcliff?” I asked.
He answered with a nod.

“Mr. Lockwood, sir, your new tenant. I have the honour of paying my respects as soon as I can after arriving, and hope I have not inconvenienced you by asking so persistently to rent Thrushcross Grange: I heard yesterday that you had been considering—”
“Thrushcross Grange belongs to me, sir,” he cut in, with a wince. “I would let nobody inconvenience me if I could prevent it—come in!”

His “come in” emerged through clenched teeth and meant, plainly enough, “Go to the Devil!” Even the gate he leaned on showed no inclination to support the invitation by moving; and I think that decided me to accept it. I was interested in a man who seemed to carry reserve even further than I did myself.

Once he saw my horse’s chest actually pressing against the gate, he reached out to unfasten its chain, then led me sullenly up the paved path. As we entered the courtyard he called, “Joseph, take Mr. Lockwood’s horse; and bring us some wine.”

“That must be the entire household staff, I suppose,” I reflected on hearing these combined instructions. “No wonder grass grows between the paving stones, and the hedges have only cattle to trim them.”

Joseph was elderly—no, old; very old, perhaps, though vigorous and wiry. “The Lord help us!” he muttered to himself in a low, peevishly disapproving voice as he took my horse. Meanwhile, he gave my face so sour a look that I generously supposed he needed divine assistance to digest his dinner, and that his pious outburst had nothing to do with my unexpected arrival.

Mr. Heathcliff’s house is called Wuthering Heights. “Wuthering” is an expressive local word for the atmospheric uproar to which its exposed position subjects it in stormy weather. They must indeed have plenty of fresh, bracing air up there at all times: you can judge the strength of the north wind sweeping over the ridge by the extreme tilt of a few stunted fir trees beside the house, and by a row of gaunt thorns stretching their branches all one way, as though begging the sun for charity. Fortunately, the architect had the foresight to make it solid: the narrow windows are set deep in the walls, and great projecting stones protect the corners.

Before stepping inside, I stopped to admire the fantastic carvings scattered lavishly across the front, particularly round the main doorway. Above it, among a wilderness of crumbling griffins and shameless little boys, I made out the date “1500” and the name “Hareton Earnshaw.” I would have offered a few observations and asked the ill-tempered owner for a brief history of the place; but his stance in the doorway seemed to demand that I either come in immediately or leave altogether. I did not want to try his patience further before inspecting the inner sanctuary.

A single step took us into the family sitting room, without any preliminary hall or passage. Here they call this principal room “the house.” It generally serves as both kitchen and parlour; but at Wuthering Heights I think the kitchen has been driven into a separate part of the building altogether. At any rate, I could hear voices chattering and cooking utensils rattling far inside, and saw no signs of roasting, boiling or baking around the enormous fireplace, nor copper pans and tin colanders shining on the walls. At one end, however, both light and heat were splendidly reflected by ranks of huge pewter dishes, with silver jugs and tankards between them, rising in row upon row on a vast oak dresser right up to the roof. There was no ceiling beneath that roof: its whole structure lay exposed to an inquisitive eye, except where a wooden rack loaded with oatcakes and bunches of legs of beef, mutton and ham hid it. Above the fireplace hung several evil-looking old guns and a pair of horse pistols; three brightly painted tins arranged on the mantelpiece supplied the decoration. The floor was smooth white stone. The chairs were primitive, high-backed things painted green, with one or two heavy black ones lurking in the shadows. A huge liver-coloured female pointer lay in an arched recess beneath the dresser, surrounded by a swarm of squealing puppies; other dogs occupied the remaining corners.

The room and its furniture would have been perfectly ordinary possessions for a plain northern farmer, a stubborn-faced man whose sturdy legs showed well in knee breeches and gaiters. You may see such a man sitting in his armchair, a mug of frothing ale on the round table before him, anywhere within five or six miles of these hills, if you arrive at the right time after dinner. But Mr. Heathcliff presents a striking contrast to his home and way of life. In appearance he is a dark-skinned gypsy; in clothes and manners, a gentleman—that is, as much of one as many a country squire. He may be somewhat untidy, but his neglect does not look bad on him, for he stands straight and has a handsome figure; and he is rather sullen. Some people might suspect a touch of ill-bred pride. Something sympathetic within me says it is nothing of the kind: I know instinctively that his reserve comes from a dislike of showy feelings—of demonstrations of mutual goodwill. He will conceal his love and hatred equally, and think it something of an impertinence to be loved or hated in return. No, I am getting ahead of myself: I am much too ready to give him my own characteristics. Mr. Heathcliff may have entirely different reasons from mine for keeping his hand out of reach when someone hopes to make his acquaintance. Let me hope that my disposition is almost unique: my dear mother used to say I would never have a comfortable home; and only last summer I proved myself completely unworthy of one.

During a month of fine weather at the seaside, I found myself in the company of a most fascinating creature: a true goddess in my eyes, so long as she took no notice of me. I “never told my love” aloud; yet, if looks can speak, the greatest idiot could have guessed that I was head over heels. At last she understood, and answered with a look—the sweetest look anyone could imagine. And what did I do? I confess it with shame: I withdrew icily into myself, like a snail. With every glance I retreated further and grew colder, until the poor innocent finally began to distrust her own senses and, overwhelmed with embarrassment at her supposed mistake, persuaded her mother to leave.
This curious twist in my character has earned me a reputation for intentional heartlessness. Only I can understand how little I deserve it.

I sat down at the opposite end of the hearth from the one my landlord approached, and tried to fill a silence by stroking the mother dog. She had left her puppies and was creeping wolfishly behind my legs, lip curled, white teeth watering for a bite. My friendly touch brought out a long growl deep in her throat.

“You’d best leave the dog alone,” Mr. Heathcliff growled in accompaniment, stopping her more threatening movements with a thrust of his foot. “She isn’t used to being fussed over—we don’t keep her as a pet.” Then he strode to a side door and shouted once more, “Joseph!”

From the depths of the cellar Joseph muttered something indistinct, but showed no sign of coming up. His master therefore plunged down after him, leaving me _vis-à-vis_ the ruffianly bitch and two grim, shaggy sheepdogs, who joined her in jealously watching every movement I made. Having no wish to meet their fangs, I kept still; but I imagined they could hardly understand insults delivered in silence, and unfortunately began winking and pulling faces at the three of them. Some twist of my features so offended madam that she flew into a sudden rage and jumped onto my knees. I threw her off and hurried to get the table between us. This action stirred up the whole hive: half a dozen four-legged devils, of different ages and sizes, came out of hidden dens and converged on the same spot. My heels and coat tails seemed particularly singled out for attack; and while I kept the bigger fighters off with the poker as well as I could, I was forced to call loudly for someone in the household to help restore peace.

Mr. Heathcliff and his servant climbed the cellar steps with infuriating calm. I doubt they moved a second faster than usual, although the hearth was a perfect storm of snapping and yelping. Fortunately someone in the kitchen acted more quickly: a vigorous woman with her dress tucked up, her arms bare and her cheeks red from the fire rushed among us brandishing a frying pan. She used this weapon and her tongue so effectively that the storm subsided as if by magic. When her master appeared, she alone remained in motion, heaving like the sea after a gale.
“What the devil is going on?” he demanded, looking me over in a way I could hardly bear after such an inhospitable reception.
“What the devil indeed!” I muttered. “The herd of possessed swine can’t have held worse spirits than these animals of yours, sir. You might as well abandon a stranger among a litter of tigers!”
“They leave people alone if people leave things alone,” he observed, setting the bottle in front of me and putting the table back. “Quite right of the dogs to keep watch. A glass of wine?”
“No, thank you.”
“You haven’t been bitten?”
“If I had, I’d have left my own mark on the biter.” Heathcliff’s face loosened into a grin.

“Come now,” he said, “you’re upset, Mr. Lockwood. Here, have a little wine. Visitors are so extraordinarily uncommon in this house that my dogs and I, I’ll readily admit, scarcely know how to welcome them. Your health, sir?”

I bowed and drank to his health in return, beginning to see how foolish it would be to sit sulking over the bad behaviour of a pack of mongrels. Besides, since his humour ran that way, I was unwilling to give the fellow any further amusement at my expense. He—probably reflecting sensibly that offending a good tenant would be foolish—relaxed somewhat his clipped manner of speech, with its missing pronouns and helping verbs, and began what he supposed would interest me: a discussion of the merits and drawbacks of my present retreat. He knew a great deal about the subjects we touched on; and by the time I left for home I felt encouraged enough to offer to visit again tomorrow. He clearly had no wish for me to intrude a second time. Nevertheless, I shall go. It is astonishing how sociable I feel when I compare myself with him.
